Whatever4 Christ was subject to that was the judicial fruit of sin had the nature of satisfaction for sin. But not only proper suffering, but all abasement and depression of the state or circumstance of mankind below its primitive honor and dignity, such as his body's remaining under death, and body and soul remaining separate, and other things that might be mentioned, are the judicial fruits of sin. And all that Christ did in his state of humiliation that had the nature of obedience, or moral virtue, or goodness in it in one respect or another, had the nature of merit in it, and was part of the price with which he purchased happiness for the elect.

-- 306 --

1SERMON FIFTEEN
[For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation form generation to generation.] Isaiah 51:8
[DOCTRINE]
[The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.]2

2.3 I would observe that both Christ's satisfaction for sin and also his meriting happiness by his righteousness were carried on through the whole time of his humiliation. Christ's satisfaction4 for sin was not only by his last sufferings, though it was principally by them. But all his sufferings, and all the humiliation that he was subject to, from the first moment of his incarnation to his resurrection, were propitiatory or satisfactory. Christ's satisfaction was chiefly by his death, because his suffering and humiliation in that was greatest, but all his other suffering and all his other humiliation all along had the nature of satisfaction. So had the mean circumstances in which he was born; his being born in such a low condition was to make satisfaction for sin. His being born of a poor virgin in a stable, and his being laid in

-- 307 --

a manger, his taking the human nature upon him in its low state, and under those infirmities brought upon it by the fall, his being born in the form of sinful flesh, had the nature of satisfaction. And so all his sufferings in his infancy and childhood, and all that labor, and contempt, and reproach, and temptation, and difficulty of some5 kind other that he suffered through the whole course of his life, was of propitiatory and satisfactory nature. And so his purchase of happiness by his righteousness was also carried on through the whole time of his humiliation till his resurrection, not only in that obedience he performed through the course of his life, but also the obedience he performed in laying down his life.

3.6 It was by the same things that Christ both satisfied God's justice and also purchased eternal happiness; this satisfaction and purchase of Christ were not only both carried on through the whole time of Christ's humiliation, but they were both carried on by the same things. He did not make satisfaction by some things that he did, and then work out righteousness by other different things; but in the same acts by which he wrought out righteousness he also made satisfaction, but only taken with a different relation. One and the same act of Christ, considered with respect to the obedience there was in it, was part of his righteousness and purchased heaven; but considered with respect to the self-denial, and difficulty, and humiliation with which he performed it, it had the nature of righteousness and merited happiness7 for us. Thus his going about doing good, preaching the gospel, and teaching disciples, was part of righteousness and purchase of heaven as it was done in obedience to the Father; and the same was part of his satisfaction as he did it with great labor, trouble, and weariness, and under great large labor, exposing himself thereby to reproach and contempt. So his laying down his life had the nature of satisfaction to God's offended justice considered as his bearing our punishment in our stead; but considered as an act of obedience to God who had given him this command that he should lay down his life for sinners it was part of his righteous purchase of heaven, and as much the principal part of his righteousness as it was the principal part of his satisfaction. And so to instance in his circumcision, what he suffered in that had the nature of satisfaction, the blood that was shed in his circumcision was propitiatory blood; but as it was a conformity

-- 308 --

to the law of Moses it was part of his meritorious righteousness.8 Though it was not9 properly the act of his human nature, he being an infant, yet it being what the human nature was the subject of, and was the act of that person, it was accepted as an act of his obedience as our mediator. And so even his being born in such a low condition, it had the nature of satisfaction by reason of the humiliation that was in it; and also of righteousness, as it was the act of his person in obedience to the Father and what the human nature was the subject of and what the will of the human nature did acquiesce in, though there was no act of the will of the human nature prior to it.

These things may suffice to have observed in the general concerning the purchase Christ made of redemption. I now proceed,

III.1 to speak more particularly of those things Christ did and was the subject of during the time of his humiliation, whereby this purchase was made. And the nature of the purchase of Christ as it has been explained leads us to2 consider these things under a twofold view, viz. 1. with respect to his righteousness that appeared in them; 2. with respect to the sufferings and humiliation that he was subject to in them in our stead.

1.3 I will consider the things that passed during the time of Christ's humiliation with respect to the obedience and righteousness that he exercised in them. And this is subject to a threefold distribution, 1. with respect [to] laws he obeyed, and 2. with respect to the different stages of his life, and 3. what virtues he exercised in that obedience.

1.4 Christ's acts of righteousness may be distributed with respect [to] the legal laws Christ obeyed in that righteousness he performed. But here it must be observed in general that all the precepts that Christ obeyed may [be] reduced to one law, and that is that which the Apostle calls "the law of works," Romans 3:27. Every command that Christ obeyed may be reduced to that great and everlasting law of God that is contained in the covenant of works, that eternal rule of righteousness that God had established between himself and mankind.

-- 309 --

Christ came into the world to fulfill and answer the covenant of works, that is the covenant that is to stand forever as a rule5 of judgment, and that is the covenant that we had broken, and that was the covenant that must be fulfilled.

This law of works indeed includes all laws of God that ever have been given to mankind, both the law of nature and also all political commands that ever were given to man; for 'tis a general rule of the law of works, and indeed of the law of nature, that God is to be obeyed and that he must be submitted to in whatever positive precept he is pleased to give us. 'Tis a rule of the law of works that men should obey their earthly parents, and 'tis certainly as much of a rule of the same law that we should obey our heavenly Father: and so the law of works requires obedience to all positive commands of God. It so required Adam's obedience to that positive command ‹not to eat of the forbidden fruit›, and it required the Jews' obedience ‹to all the positive commands given them›. When God commanded Jonah to arise and go to Nineveh, the law of works required ‹him to obey›. And so it required Christ's obedience to all the positive commands God gave him. But more particularly, the commands of God that Christ obeyed were of three kinds: they were either such as he was subject to merely as man, or such6 as he was subject to as he was a Jew, or such as he was subject to purely as mediator.

1.7 He obeyed those commands that he was subject to merely as man, and they were the commands of the moral law, which was the same with that that was given at Mount Sinai, written in two tables of stone, which are of obligation to mankind of all nations and all ages of the world.

2.8 He obeyed all those laws that he was subject to as he was a Jew. Thus he was subject to ceremonial law and was conformed to it. He was conformed to it in his being circumcised the eighth day. And he strictly obeyed it in going up to Jerusalem to the temple three times in the year, at least after he was come to the age of twelve years, which seems to have been the age when the males began to go up to the temple. And so Christ constantly attended the service of the temple and of the synagogues.

To the head of his obedience to the laws that he was subject to as

-- 310 --

a Jew may be reduced his submission to John's baptism; for it was a special command of God to the Jews to go forth9 to John the Baptist and be baptized of him. And therefore Chirst, being a Jew, was subject to this command, and therefore when he came to be baptized of John, and John objected that he had more need to come to him be baptized of him, he gives this reason for it: that it was needful that he should do it that he might fulfill all righteousness, Matthew 3:13–15 ["Then cometh Jesus … unto John, to be baptized of him. But John forbad him, saying … comest thou to me? And Jesus answering said … it becometh us to fulfill all righteousness"].

3.1 Another law that Christ was subject to was the mediatorial law which contained those commands of God that he was subject to, not merely as man, nor yet as a Jew, but related purely to the execution of his mediatorial office. Such were the commands that the Father gave him to teach such doctrines, to preach the gospel, to work such miracles, to call such disciples, to appoint such ordinances, and finally to lay down his life. For Christ did all these things in obedience to commands that he had received of the Father, as he often tells us.2 And these commands he was not subject to merely as man, for they did not belong to other men; nor yet3 was he subject to 'em as Jew, for they were no part of the Mosaic law. But they were commands that he had received of the Father that purely respected the work he was to do in the world in his mediatorial office.

And 'tis to be observed that Christ's righteousness, by which he merited heaven for himself and all that believe in him, consists principally in his obedience to this mediatorial law: for in fulfilling this law consisted his chief work and business in the world. The history of the Evangelists4 is chiefly taken up in giving an account of his obedience to this law. And this part of his obedience was that which was attended with the greatest difficulty of all, and therefore his obedience in it was most meritorious.

What Christ had to do in the world by virtue of his being mediator was infinitely more difficult than what he had to do merely as man or as a Jew. To his obedience to this mediatorial [law] belongs his

-- 311 --

going through his last sufferings, beginning with his agony in the garden and ending ‹with his resurrection›. As the obedience of the Adam, wherein his righteousness would have consisted5 if he had stood, would have mainly consisted not in his obedience to the moral law that he was subject to merely as man, but in his obedience to that special law that he was subject to as a moral head and surety of mankind, even the command of abstaining from the tree of knowledge ‹of good and evil›, so the obedience of the second Adam, wherein his righteousness consists, lies mainly not in his obedience to the law that he was subject to merely as man, but to that special law, that which he was subject [to] in his office as mediator and surety for man.6

Before7 I proceed to the next distribution of Christ's righteousness I would observe three things concerning Christ's obedience to these laws.

1.8 He performed that obedience to them that was in every respect perfect. It was universal as to the kinds of laws that he was subject [to]; he obeyed each of these three laws. And it was universal with respect to every individual precept contained in these laws, and it was perfect [as] to each command.

It was perfect with respect to positive transgressions avoided, for he never transgressed9 in one instance; he was guilty of no sin of commission. And it was perfect with respect to the work commanded; he perfected the whole work that each command required, and never was guilty of any sin of omission. And it was perfect with respect to the principle he acted from, which he obeyed. His heart was perfect, his principles were wholly right, there was no corruption in his heart, and it was perfect with respect to the ends he acted for; for he never had any beyond but aimed perfectly at such ends as the law of God required.

And it was perfect with respect to the manner of performance; every circumstance of each act was perfectly conformed to the command. And it was perfect with respect to the degree of the performance;

-- 312 --

he acted holy, up to the rule. And it was perfect with respect to the constancy of obedience; he did not only perfectly obey sometimes, but constantly, without any interruption. And it was perfect with respect to perseverance; he held in perfect obedience to the very end, through all the changes he passed1 through, and all the trials there were before him.

The meritoriousness of Christ's obedience depends on the perfection of it. If it had failed in any instance of perfection, it could not have been meritorious; for imperfect obedience is not accepted as any obedience at all in the sight of the law of works, which was that law that Christ was subject to. For that is not accepted as an obedience to a law that don't answer that law.2

2.3 The next thing I would observe of Christ's obedience is that it was performed through the greatest trials and temptations that ever any obedience was. His obedience was attended with the greatest difficulties, and most extreme abasement and sufferings, that ever any obedience was; which was another thing that rendered it more meritorious and thankworthy. To obey another when his commands are easy is not so worthy as 'tis to obey when it can't be done without great difficulty.

3.4 He performed this obedience with infinite respect to God and the honor of his law. The obedience he performed was with infinitely5 greater love to God and regard to his authority than the angels perform their obedience. The angels perform their obedience with love that is perfect, with sinless perfection. But Christ did not only do so, but he performed his obedience with much greater love than the angels do theirs, even infinite love. For though the human nature of Christ was not capable of love absolutely infinite, yet Christ's obedience that performed in that human nature is not to be looked on as merely the obedience of the human, but the obedience of his person as God-man, and there was infinite love of the person of Christ manifest in that obedience. And this together with the infinite dignity of the person that obeyed rendered his obedience infinitely meritorious.

[The]6 second distribution of the acts of Christ's obedience may be

-- 313 --

with respect to the different parts of his life wherein they were. And so the distribution may be into those that were performed during his Private life or his public ministry.

1.7 Those acts he performed during his private life. He was perfectly obedient in8 his childhood. He infinitely differed from other children who, as soon as they begin to act, ‹do so in disobedience›. He was subject to his earthly parents though he was Lord of all, Luke 2:51. He was found about his Father's business at twelve years of age in the temple, Luke 2:42.9 He then began that work that he had to do in fulfillment of the mediatorial law that the Father had given him. He continued his private life for about thirty years, dwelling at Nazareth in the house of his reputed father, Joseph, where he served God in a private capacity, and in following a mechanical trade, the business of a carpenter.

2.1 Those acts that he performed during his public ministry, which began when he was about thirty years of age. Thirty years was the age at which the prophet's work by God's direction began, Numbers 4, 2 and continued for the three last years and one-half of his life. Most of the history of the Evangelists is taken up in giving an account of what passed during these three years and one-half. So is all the history of the evangelist Matthew, excepting the Matthew 1–2. So is the whole of the history of the evangelist3 Mark; it begins and ends with it. And so also is all the Gospel of John, and all the Gospel of Luke, excepting the Luke 1–2, excepting what we find in the Evangelists concerning the ministry of John the Baptist. Christ's first appearing in his public ministry is what is often called his coming in Scripture.4 Thus John speaks of Christ's coming as what is yet to be, though he had been born long before.5

Concerning the public ministry of Christ, I would observe the following things: 1. the forerunner of it, 2. the manner of his entering on it, 3. the works in which he was employed during the course of it, and 4.6 the manner of his finishing of it.

-- 314 --

1.7 The forerunner of Christ's coming in his public ministry was John the Baptist.8 He came preaching repentance for the remission of sins,9 to make way for Christ's coming agreeable to the prophecies of him, Isaiah 40:3–5 ["The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord.… And the glory of the Lord shall be revealed"], and Malachi 4:5–6 ["Behold I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the … day of the Lord"]. 'Tis supposed that John the Baptist began his ministry about three years and onehalf before Christ, so that John's ministry and Christ's put together made seven years, which was the last of Daniel's weeks, Daniel 9:27, "He will confirm the covenant with many for one week," Christ came in the midst of this, viz. the beginning of the last half of it, or the last three years and one-half, as Daniel foretold, as in the same verse ["And in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease"].

John's baptizing ministry consisted principally in preaching the law to awaken men and convince 'em of sin, to prepare men for the coming of Christ to comfort 'em, as the law is to prepare the heart for the entertainment of the gospel. There was a very remarkable outpouring of the Spirit of God attended John's ministry.1 John is spoken of as the greatest of all the prophets that came before Christ, Matthew 11:11, "Among these that are born of women [there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist],"2 i.e. he had the most honorable office.

He was as the morning star that is the harbinger of the approaching day and forerunner of the rising sun. The other prophets were stars that were to give light in the night, but we have heard how those stars went out on the approach of the gospel day. But now the coming of Christ being very nigh, the morning star comes before him, the brightest of all the stars, as John the Baptist was the greatest of all the prophets. And when Christ came in his public ministry, the light of that morning star decreased too, as we see when the sun rises it diminishes the light of the morning star. So John the Baptist says of himself, John 3:30, "He must increase, but3 I must decrease." And

-- 315 --

soon after Christ began his public ministry, John the Baptist was put to death, as though the morning star is visible a little while after the sun is risen, yet soon after it goes out.

2.4 The next thing to be taken notice of is Christ's entrance on his public ministry, which was by baptism followed with the temptation in the wilderness. His baptism was, as it were, his solemn inauguration and by which he entered on his ministry; and was attended with his anointing with the Holy [Spirit], in a solemn and visible manner, the Holy Spirit descending [upon him "like a dove"],5 attended with "a voice from heaven, [saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased],"6 Matthew 3:16–17. After this he was led of the devil into the wilderness.7 Satan made a violent onset upon him in his first entrance on his work, and now he had a remarkable trial of his obedience. But he got the victory.8 He who had such success with the first Adam had none with the second.

3.9 I would take notice of the works in which Christ was employed during the course of his ministry. And here are three things chiefly to be taken notice of, viz. his preaching, and his working miracles, his calling and appointing disciples, ministers of his kingdom.

1.1 His preaching the gospel. Great part of the work of his public ministry consisted in this, and much of that obedience by which he purchased salvation for us was in his speaking those things that the Father commanded him. He more clearly and abundantly revealed the mind and will of God than ever it had been before. He came from the "bosom of the Father,"2 and perfectly knew his mind, and was under the best capacity to reveal it. As the sun as soon as 'tis risen begins to shine, so Christ as soon as he came into his public ministry began to enlighten the world with his doctrine.3 As the law was given at Mount Sinai, so Christ delivered his blessed evangelical doctrine to a multitude on a mountain, full of blessings and not torments and curses, as we have an account in the Matthew 5–7.4

-- 316 --

He when he preached he did not teach as the scribes but he taught "as one having authority,"5 so that his hearers were astonished at his doctrine. He did not reveal the mind and will of God in the style that the prophets used to. The prophets don't used to preach as speaking their own word, but the word of another; and used to speak in such a style as this, "Thus saith the Lord," but Christ in such a style as this, "I say unto you" thus or thus, "verily, verily, I say unto you."6 He delivered his doctrines not only as the doctrines of God the Father, but as his own doctrines. He gave forth his commands, not as the prophets used to as God's commands, but as his own commands. He spoke in7 such a style as this, John 15:12, 8 "This is my commandment," then are ye my disciples "if ye do whatsoever I command you,"9 John 15:14.

2.1 Another thing that Christ was employed in during the course of his ‹ministry› was working miracles, concerning which I would observe several things:

1.2 There [were] multitudes. Besides particular instances we often have an account of multitudes coming with diseases, and his healing them all.

2.3 They were works of mercy.

3.4 They were almost all of them such as had been spoken of as the peculiar works5 of God in the Old Testament: Stilling the sea,6 Psalms 107:29, "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still." Walking on the sea in a storm,7 Job 9:8 "Which [alone …

-- 317 --

treadeth upon the waves of the sea]." Casting out devils,8 Psalms 74:14, "Thou brakest [the heads of leviathan in pieces]." Feeding a multitude in a wilderness,9 Deuteronomy 8:16, "Who fed thee in a wilderness [with manna]." Telling man's thoughts,1 Amos 4:13 ["Lo, he that … declareth unto man what is his thought"]. Raising the dead,2 Psalms 68:20, "Unto the Lord our God belong [the issues from death]." Opening eyes of blind,3 Psalms 146:8, "The Lord openeth the eyes of the blind." Healing sick,4 Psalms 103:3, "Who healeth all thy [diseases]." Lifting up them who are bowed and bound together,5 Psalms 146:7–8, 6 "The Lord looseth the prisoners: he raiseth up them that there are bowed down."

4.7 They were in general such works as were images of the great work he came to work on man's heart.

5.8 He wrought them in such a manner as to show that he did 'em by his own power, and not by the power of another, as9 other prophets did in the name of the Lord. Moses was forbidden to enter into Canaan because he seemed by his speech to assume the honor of working [one miracle only by himself],1 not as the apostles did who wrought all in the name of Christ. [Christ] wrought in his own name, by his own authority and will: "I will; [be thou clean]," Matthew 8:3, Matthew 9:28, "Believe ye that I am able [to do this?]."

3.2 The next thing that Christ did ‹in the course of his public ministry› was the calling disciples. He called many disciples. There

-- 318 --

were many that he prepared as ministers; seventy disciples [were] sent forth.3 But there were twelve that he set apart as apostles that were to be the grand ministers of his kingdom, as twelve foundations of his church, Revelation 21:14, [to] sit on twelve thrones [as] main instruments of setting up his kingdom in the world.

4.4 I would observe how he finished, and this was: 1. in giving his dying counsels to his disciples and all that be his disciples,5 2. in instituting a solemn memorial of his death,6 3. as God's high priest, offering up himself a sacrifice to God, which he did in his last sufferings.7 This he did as God's minister, as God's anointed priest; and it was the greatest act of his public ministry, the greatest act of his obedience by which he purchased heaven for believers. The priests of old used to do many other things as God's ministers, but then were they in their highest execution of their office when they were actually offering sacrifice on the altar. So the greatest thing that Christ did in the execution of his office, and the greatest thing that ever he did and the greatest thing that ever was done, was the offering up [himself a sacrifice to God].8 Herein he was the antitype of all that had been done, by all the priests, and in all their sacrifices and offerings, from the beginning of the world.

-- 319 --

1No. 6: SERMON SIXTEEN June 17, 17392
[For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation from generation to generation.] Isaiah 51:8
[DOCTRINE]
[The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.]3

IN showing from this text how that the Work of Redemption is carried on from the fall of man to the end of the world, after having shown how it was carried on through that period from the fall of man to the incarnation of Christ, we were last showing how it was carried on through the second period, viz. from the incarnation of Christ till his resurrection, from this proposition: [that during the time of Christ's humiliation, from his incarnation to his resurrection, the purchase of redemption was made].4 And in how by this I proposed: first, to consider the incarnation by which Christ qualified; 2. to consider the purchase itself. And in speaking of the purchase itself, three things were proposed, 1. show what is intended by the purchase of redemption, 2. observe some things in general concerning those things by which the purchase was made, 3. and duly consider two more particulars to those things that Christ did and suffered by which that purchase was made.

We entered in a third and last of these things proposed, viz. a more particular consideration of those things by which the purchase was

-- 320 --

made. And here it was proposed to consider those things under a twofold view, viz. 1. with respect to his righteousness that appeared in them, and 2. with respect to the suffering and humiliation that he was subject to in them in our stead. And in considering them with respect to his righteousness that5 appears in them, it was observed that they were subject to a threefold distribution, viz., 1. with respect to the laws he obeyed, 2. with respect to the different stages of life, 3. with respect to the virtues he manifested. I have considered those things by which Christ purchased redemption as by a righteousness with regard to the two former. I now come,

3.6 to consider 'em in the last place with regard to the virtues that Christ exercised and manifested in them. And here I would observe that Christ in doing the work that he had to do here in the world for our redemption exercised every possible virtue and grace. Indeed there are some particular virtues that sinful man may have that were not in Christ, not from any want or defect of virtue, but because his virtue was perfect and without defect. Such is the virtue of repentance, and brokenness of heart for sin, and mortification, and denying lust. These virtues were not in Christ because he had no sin of his own to repent of, nor any lust to deny. But all virtues that don't presuppose sin7 were in him, and that in a higher degree than ever they were in any other man or any mere creature. Every virtue in him was perfect. Virtue itself was greater in him than in any other, and it was under greater advantages to shine in him than in any other. Strict virtue shines most when most tried, but never any virtue had such trials as Christ's had.

The virtue that Christ exercised in the work that he did may be divided into three sorts, viz. the virtues that more immediately respect God, himself, and men.

1.8 Those virtues that more immediately respect God wonderfully appeared in Christ in the work that he did for our redemption. There appeared in him a holy fear and reverence towards God the Father. Christ had a greater trial of his virtue in this respect than ever any other had, from the honorableness of his person. This was the temptation of the angels that fell, to cast off their worship of God and reverence of his majesty, that they were beings of such exalted dignity

-- 321 --

and worthiness themselves. But Christ was infinitely more worthy and honorable than they, for he was the eternal son of God and his person was equal to the person of God the Father; and yet as he had taken on him the office of a mediator and the nature of man, he was full of9 reverence towards God. He adored him in the most reverential manner time after time.

So he manifested a wonderful love to God. The angels give great testimonies of their love to God in their constancy and activity in doing the will of God. And many saints have given great testimonies of their love, who from love to God have endured great labors and sufferings. But none ever gave such testimonies of love to God as Christ has done, none ever performed such a labor of love as he, or suffered so much from love to God as he. So he manifested the most wonderful submission to the will of God. Never was anybody's submission so tried as his was. So he manifested the most wonderful spirit of obedience that ever was manifested. And then,

2.1 Christ in this work wonderfully manifested those virtues that more immediately respected himself, as particularly humility and patience, contempt of the world. Christ though he was the most excellent and honorable of all men, yet was the most humble. Yea, he was the most humble of all creatures. No angels nor men ever equaled him in humility though he was the highest of all creatures in dignity and honorableness. Christ would have been under the greatest temptations to pride if it had been possible that anything could have been a2 temptation to him. The temptation of the angels that fell was the dignity of their nature and the honorableness of their circumstances, but Christ was infinitely more honorable than they. The human nature of Christ was so honored as to be in the same person with the eternal son of God, that was equal with God, and yet that human nature was not at all lifted up with pride. Nor was the man, Christ Jesus, at all lifted up with pride with all those wonderful works [such as] raising the dead. And though he knew that God had appointed him to be the king over heaven and earth, angels and men, as he says, Matthew 11:27, "All things are delivered unto me [of my Father]," though he knew he was such an infinitely honorable person, and "thought it not robbery [to be equal with God],"3 and though he knew

-- 322 --

he was the heir of God the Father's kingdom, yet such was his humility that he did not disdain to be abased and depressed down into lower and viler circumstances and sufferings than ever any other elect creature was; so that he became least of all and lowest of all. The proper trial and evidence of humility is stooping or complying with those acts or circumstances4 when called to it that are very low and contain great abasement. But none ever stooped so low as Christ, if we consider either the infinite height that he stooped from, or the great depth to which he stooped. Such was his humility that though he knew his infinite worthiness of honor, and of being honored ten thousand times as much as the highest prince on earth, or angel in heaven yet he did not think it too much when called to it to be bound as a cursed malefactor, and to be the laughing stock and spitting stock of the vilest of men, and to be crowned with thorns and a mock robe5 and crucified like a slave and malefactor and one of the meanest and worst of vagabonds and miscreants, and a cursed enemy of God and men that was not fit to live on the earth, and that not for himself but for some of the meanest and vilest of creatures, some of those cursed wretches that crucified [him]. Was not this a wonderful manifestation of humility when he cheerfully and most freely complied with this abasement.

And how did his patience shine forth under all the terrible sufferings6 he endured when he was dumb and opened not his mouth but went as a lamb to the slaughter.7 And was like a patient lamb under all the sufferings he endured from first to last. And what contempt of the glory of the world was there when he rather chose this contempt and meanness and suffering, than to wear a temporal crown and be invested with the external glories of an earthly prince, as the multitude often solicited him.8

3.9 Christ in the work that he wrought out, in a wonderful manner exercised those virtues that more immediately respect other men. And these may be summed up under two heads, viz. meekness and love.

Christ's meekness was his humble calmness of spirit under the

-- 323 --

provocations that he met with. None ever met with so great provocations as he did. The greatness of provocation lies in two things, viz. in the degree of opposition by which the provocation is given, and secondly in the degree of the unreasonableness of that opposition,1 or in its being very causeless and without reason, and the great degree of obligation to the contrary.

Now if we consider both these things, no man ever met with such provocations as Christ did when he was upon earth. If we consider how much he was hated, what abuses he suffered from the vilest of men, how great his sufferings from men were, and how spiteful and how contemptuous they were in offering him these abuses; and also consider how causeless and unreasonable these abuses were, how undeserving he was of them, and how much deserving of the contrary, viz. of love, and honor, and good treatment at their hands, I say, if we consider these things, no man ever met with a thousandth part of the provocation that Christ met with from men. And yet how meek was he under all, how composed and quiet his spirit, how far from being in a ruffle and tumult; when he was reviled he reviled not. Again, Isaiah 53:7, "as a sheep before his shearers is dumb, so he opened not his mouth." No appearance of a2 revengeful spirit; on the contrary, what a spirit of forgiveness was there. So that he fervently and effectually prayed for their forgiveness when they were in the highest act of provocation that ever they were, viz. nailing him to the cross, Luke 23:34, "Father forgive."3

And never did there appear such an instance of love to men, Christ's love to men, that he showed when on earth. And especially in going through his last sufferings and offering up his life and soul under those sufferings, which was his greatest act of love; [this] was far beyond all parallel. There have been very remarkable manifestions of love in some of the saints, as in the apostle Paul, the apostle John, and others, but the love to men that Christ showed when on earth as much exceeded the love of all other men as the ocean exceeds a small stream.

And 'tis to be observed that all the virtues that appeared in Christ shone brightest in the close of his life under the trials he met with then. Eminent virtue always shines brightest in the fire, pure gold

-- 324 --

shows its purity chiefly in the furnace.4 It was chiefly under those trials that Christ underwent in the close of his life that his love to God, his honor of God's majesty, and his regard to honor of his law, and his spirit of obedience, and his humility, and contempt of the world, and his patience, and his meekness, and spirit of forgiveness, and love towards men appeared. Indeed everything that Christ did to work out redemption for us appears mainly in the close of his life. Here mainly is his satisfaction for sin, and here chiefly lies his merit of eternal life for sinners, and here chiefly appears the brightness of his example that he hath set us to follow.

Thus we have taken a brief view of the things whereby the purchase of redemption was made with respect to his righteousness that appeared in them. I proceed now,

II.5 To take a view of them with regard to the satisfaction that he thereby made for sin, or the sufferings and humiliation that he was the subject of in them on our account. And here,

1.6 He was subject to uncommon humiliation and sufferings in his infancy. He was born to that end that he might die, and therefore he did, as it7 were, begin to die as soon as he was born. His mother suffered in an uncommon manner in bearing him. When her travail came upon her, 'tis said "there was no room for her in the inn," Luke 2:7. She was forced to betake herself to a stable, and therefore Christ was born in the place of the bringing forth of beasts. Thus he suffered in his birth as though he had [been] meaner and viler than a man, and not possessed of the dignity of the human nature, but had been of the rank of the brute creatures. And we may conclude that his mother's circumstances in other respects were proportionably strait and difficult, and that she was destitute of the conveniences necessary for a newborn infant that others were wont to have; for want of which the newborn babe, without doubt, suffered much.

And then he was persecuted in his infancy. They began to seek his life as soon as he was born. Herod, the chief man in the land, was so engaged to kill him that in order to it he killed all the children in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under.8 And Christ suffered banishment in his infancy, was driven

-- 325 --

out of his native country into Egypt, and without doubt suffered9 much by being carried so long a journey when he was so young, into a strange country.1

And,

22 Christ was subject to such great humiliation in his private life at Nazareth. He there led a servile, obscure life in a mean, laborious occupation; for he is called not only the carpenter's son, but the carpenter, Mark 6:3, "Is not this the carpenter, the brother of James, and Joses and Juda and Simon."3 He by hard labor earned his bread before he eat it, and so suffered that curse that God pronounced on Adam, Genesis 3:19, "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread."

Let us consider how great a degree of humiliation the glorious Son of God, the creator of heaven and earth, was subject to in this: that for about thirty years together he should live a private, obscure life among laboring men, and all this while to be overlooked, and not taken notice of in the world, as more than other common laborers. Christ's humiliation in some respects was greater in his private life than in the time of his public ministry. For in his public ministry there was many manifestations of his glory in the word he preached, and the great miracles he wrought. But the first thirty years of his life he spent among mean, ordinary men, as it4 were, in silence, without those manifestations of his glory or anything to make him to be taken notice of more than any ordinary mechanic, but only the spotless purity and eminent holiness of his life, and that was in a great measure hid in obscurity so that he was little taken notice till after his baptism.

3.5 Christ was the subject of great humiliation and suffering during his public life from his baptism till the night wherein he was betrayed. As particularly,

1.6 He suffered great poverty so that he had not "where to lay his head," Matthew 8:20, and commonly used to lodge abroad in the open air for want of a shelter to betake himself to, as you will see is manifest

-- 326 --

if you compare the following places together which I shall but name to you: even Matthew 8:20, and John 18:1–2, and Luke 21:37, and Luke 22:39. So that what is spoken of Christ in Canticles 5:2, "My head is [filled] with dew and my locks [with the drops of the night]" was literally ‹fulfilled›. And through his poverty he doubtless was often7 pinched with hunger and cold.8 His mother and natural relations were poor and not able to help him. And Christ was maintained by the charity of some of his disciples while he lived. So we read in Luke 8, at beginning,9 of certain women that followed him and "ministered to him of their substance." He was so poor that he was not able to pay the tribute that was demanded of him without the miracle of creating a fish to bring the money out of the sea in his mouth, Matthew 17:27. And when he eat his last passover it was not at his own charge, but at the charge of another, as appears by Luke 22:7 etc. ["And he sent Peter and John, saying, Go and prepare us the passover.… And they said unto him, Where wilt thou that we prepare? And he said … there shall a man meet you … follow him into the house where he entereth in. And ye shall say unto the goodman of the house, The Master saith unto thee, Where is the guest chamber, where I shall eat the passover with my disciples?"].1 And from his poverty he had no grave of his own to be buried in. It was the manner of the Jews, unless they were very poor and were not able, to prepare 'em a sepulcher to be buried in while they lived. But Christ had no land of his own though he was possessor of heaven and earth, and therefore was buried by Joseph of Arimathaea's charity, in his tomb that he had prepared for himself.2

2.3 He suffered great hatred and reproach. He was "despised and rejected of men":4 he was by most esteemed a poor, insignificant5 person, one of little account, slighted for his low parentage and his mean city, Nazareth.6 He was reproached as a glutton and drunkard,7 and a friend of publicans and sinners;8 was called a deceiver of the

-- 327 --

people; sometimes was called a madman and a Samaritan, and possessed with the devil, John 7:20, John 8:48 and John 10:20. He was called a blasphemer,9 and accounted by many a wizard or one that wrought miracles by the black art and by communication with Beelzebub.1 They excommunicated him, and agreed to excommunicate any man that should own him, as John 9:22. They wished him dead, and were continually seeking to murder him, sometimes by force and sometimes by craft. They often took up stones to stone him, and once led him to the brow of an hill, intending to throw him down the precipice, to dash him in pieces against the rocks.2 He was thus hated and reproached by his own visible people, John 1:11, "He came to his own and his own received3 him not." And he was principally despised and hated by those that were in chief repute and were their greatest men. And the hatred wherewith he was hated was general; into whatever part of the land he went he met with hatred and contempt: in Capernaum, when he went to Jericho, to Jerusalem the holy city, to the temple there, Nazareth his own city, and among his relations and old neighbors.

34 He suffered the buffetings of the devil in an uncommon manner. We read of one time in particular when he had a long conflict with the devil; when he was in the wilderness forty days with nothing but wild beasts and devils, and was so exposed to the devil's power that he was bodily carried about by him from place to place while he was otherwise in a very suffering state.5

And so much for the humiliation and suffering of Christ's public life from his baptism to the night wherein he was betrayed.6 I come now,

4.7 to his last humiliation and sufferings, from the evening of the night wherein he was betrayed to his resurrection. And here was his greatest humiliation and suffering, by which principally it was that he made satisfaction to the justice of God for the sins of men.

And in the first place, his life was sold by one of his disciples for

-- 328 --

thirty pieces of silver, which was the price of the life of a servant, as you may see, Exodus 21:32.8

And then after this, Christ was in that dreadful agony in the garden. There came such a dismal gloom upon the soul of Christ that he began to be sorrowful and very heavy, and said, his "soul was exceeding sorrowful even unto death," and was sore amazed.9 And so violent was the agony of his soul as to force the blood through the pores of his skin, so that while his soul was overwhelmed with amazing sorrow his body was all blotted with blood.1

And the disciples, that used to be as his friends, and family at this time above all appearing2 cold towards him and unconcerned for him at the same time that his Father's face was hid from him. And then Judas that Christ had been so very merciful to, and treated as one of his family or familiar friends, comes and betrays him in a most deceitful, treacherous manner.3 And then the officers and soldiers apprehend him and bind him.4 And then his disciples forsake him and flee; his own best friends don't stand by him, to comfort him in this, his time of distress.5 And then he was led away as a malefactor to appear before the priests and scribes, his venomous mortal enemies, that they might sit as his judges; who sat up all night to have the pleasure of insulting him now they had got him into their hands, and spent the remaining part of the night in abusing him.6 But because they aimed at nothing short of life, they set themselves to find some color7 to put him to death, and seek for witnesses against him.8

And when none appeared, they set some to9 bear false witness; and when their witnesses did not agree together, then they go to examining him to catch something out of his own mouth.1 They hoped he would say that he was the Son of God, and then they thought they should have enough. But because they see they were not like to obtain

-- 329 --

it from him,2 they then go to force him to say it by adjuring him in the name [of God].3 And when he confessed that he was, then they supposed they had enough. And then it was a time of rejoicing with 'em, which they show by falling upon Christ, and spitting in his face, and blindfolding him, and striking him in the face with the palms of their hands, and then bid him prophesy (who it was that struck him), ridiculing him for pretending to be a prophet. And the very servants have a hand in the sport, Mark 14:65.4 During the sufferings of that night Peter, one of the chief of his own disciples, instead of standing by him to comfort him, appears ashamed to own him, and denies and renounces him with oaths and curses.5

And after the priests and elders had finished the6 night in so shamefully abusing him, when the morning which was the morning of the most wonderful day that ever was came, they led him away to Pilate to be condemned to death by him, because they had not the power of life and death in their own hands. And then he was brought before Pilate's judgment seat, and there the priests and elders accuse him as a traitor.7 And when Pilate upon examining into the matter declared he find no fault in him, the Jews were but the more fierce and violent to have him condemned. Upon which Pilate after clearing him, very unjustly brings him upon a second trial; and then not finding any thing against him, acquits him again. Pilate treats him as a poor, worthless fellow, but is ashamed on so little pretense to condemn him as a traitor.8

And then he was sent to Herod to be tried by him. And was brought before Herod's judgment seat, and his enemies followed, and virulently accuse him before Herod. Herod don't condemn him as a traitor,

-- 330 --

or one that would set up for a king, but looks upon him as Pilate did, as a poor worthless creature not worthy to be taken notice of; and does but make9 a mere laugh of the Jews accusing him as a dangerous person to Caesar, as one that was in danger of setting up to [be] a king against him. And therefore, in derision dresses him up in a mock robe, and makes sport of him, and sends him back through the streets of Jerusalem to Pilate with his mock robe on.1

And then the Jews prefer Barabbas before him, and are instant and violent with loud voices to Pilate to crucify him. And so Pilate, after he had cleared him twice and Herod once, very unrighteously brings him on trial the third time, to try if he could not find something against him sufficient to crucify him.2

And then, Christ was stripped and scourged; thus he gave his back to the smiter.3 And then after that, though Pilate still declared that he found no fault in him, yet so unjust was he that for fear of the Jews he delivered Christ to 'em to be crucified.4 But before they execute it, his spiteful, cruel enemies take the pleasure of another5 spate of mocking him; they get round him and make a set business of [it]: stripped,6 a scarlet robe, a reed,7 a crown of thorns.8

And then Jews and Roman soldiers all together: bow the knee, spit, take the reed; and then lead him away to crucify him, and make him carry his own cross till he sunk under it, his strength being spent; and then laid it on one Simon, a Cyrenian.9

And then they execute the sentence. They nail him to the cross. And now Christ's sufferings come to the extremity, now the cup is come.1 This used to be in those days the most tormenting kind of

-- 331 --

death. No death wherein he [who]2 dies [endures] so much of men's torment; the Roman word for torment [is] taken from it.

And besides what he endured in his body, he endured vastly more in his soul.3 Now was that "travail of his soul"; it pleased God to bruise him—poured out his soul unto death, as in the Isaiah 53.4 If the forethought of this cup made him sweat blood, ‹how much more it affected his soul›. Many martyrs have endured much in body but [with] joyful souls. Christ did not sweat blood in his sufferings because his blood had went otherwise. But though he did not sweat blood, yet such was the suffering of his soul, that probably [it] rent his vitals, a literal fulfillment of that in Psalms 22:14, "I am poured out like water … my heart is melted like wax; [it is melted in the midst of my bowels]." The Jews still mock. The devil probably tormented. Luke 22:53, "This is your hour."5 Under these sufferings Christ, after having cried out once, and again,6 at [his] last hour said, "It is finished," John 19:30, "bowed the head and gave up the ghost."

And thus was finished the greatest and most wonderful thing. Now the angels beheld the most wonderful sight that ever [was]; the main thing that had been pointed at by the ceremonial law, all typical dispensations, all sacrifices, from the beginning of the world.

And Christ being thus brought under the power of death continued under [it] till the morning of the next day but one. And then was finished that great work, the purchase of our redemption, that such great preparation had been made for from the beginning of the world. Then was finished all that was required in order to satisfy the threatenings of the law, all in order to satisfy divine justice, the utmost that vindictive justice demanded, [the] whole debt paid. Then finished the whole of the purchase of eternal life. And now there is no more need of anything more [to] be done towards a purchase of salvation for sinners, nor has ever anything been done since, nor ever will anything more be done, for ever and ever.

-- 332 --

1SERMON SEVENTEEN
[For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation from generation to generation.] Isaiah 51:8
[DOCTRINE]
[The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.]2

THE subject that we have been upon from the text being God's carrying on ‹the Work of Redemption from the fall of man to the end of the world›, we have now shown how this work was carried on through the two former of the three main periods into which this whole space of time was divided, and have brought our discourse down to the end of the time of Christ's humiliation. The proposition that we last insisted on was this, viz. that during the time of Christ's humiliation, from his incarnation to his resurrection, the purchase of redemption was accomplished. I have particularly considered and explored the subject of this proposition, and have shown how the purchase of redemption was made and finished in this space of time.3

[APPLICATION]

4I now would make some application of this proposition as taken with the preceding, i.e. I would make improvement of these two

-- 333 --

things considered conjunctly, viz. that Christ finished the purchase of redemption while in his state of humiliation here on earth, and that from the first fall of man to the coming of Christ God was preparing the way for his so doing. And this I would do,

I.5 In a use of reproof of three things: 1. of unbelief, 2. self-righteousness, and 3. a careless neglect of the salvation of Christ.

First.6 If it be as we have heard, how greatly do these things reprove those that don't believe in but reject the Lord Jesus Chirist, i.e. all those that don't heartily receive him. Persons may receive him in profession, and carry well outwardly towards him, and may wish that they had some of those benefits that Christ has purchased, and yet their hearts not receive Christ. They may [be] hearty in nothing that they do towards Christ; they may have no high esteem of Christ, nor7 any sincere honor or respect to Christ. They may be those that never yet opened the door of their heart to Christ, but have kept him shut out all their days, ever since they first heard of Christ, and his salvation has been offered to them. Though their hearts have been opened to others, their doors have been flung wide open to 'em, and they have had free admittance at all times, and have been embraced and made much of, and the best room of their hearts have been given 'em, and the throne of their hearts has been allowed 'em; yet Christ has always been shut out, and they have been deaf to all his knocks and calls. They never could find any inclination of heart to receive him, nor would they ever trust on him.

Let me now call upon you with whom it is thus, to consider how great your sin in thus rejecting Jesus Christ appears to be, from those things that have been said. You slight that glorious person for whose coming God made such great preparation, in such a series of wonderful providences from the beginning of the world, and whom, after all things were8 ready, God sent into the world, bringing to pass a before unknown thing, viz. the union of the divine with the human nature in one person. You are guilty of slighting that great savior who after such preparation actually accomplished the purchase of redemption; and also after he had spent three or four and thirty years in poverty and labor and contempt in purchasing redemption, at last finished the purchase by closing his life under such extreme

-- 334 --

sufferings as you have heard; and so by his death, and continuing for a time under the power of death, completed the whole. This is the person you reject and despise. You make light of all the glory of his person, and of all the glorious love of God the Father in sending him into the world, and all his wonderful love appearing in the whole of this affair.

That precious stone that God hath laid in Zion for a foundation in such a manner and by such wonderful works as you have heard, is a stone set at nought by you.9 Sinners sometimes are ready to wonder why the sin of unbelief should be looked upon as such a great sin. But if you consider what you have heard, how can you wonder? If it be so that this person be so great a savior, and this work be so great a work, and such great things have been done in order to it: truly there is no cause to wonder that the sin of unbelief, or rejection of this savior, is spoken of in Scripture as such a dreadful sin, so provoking to God, and what brings greater guilt than the sins of the worst of the heathen that never heard of these things, nor have had this savior offered to them.1

2.2 What has been said affords matter of reproof to those who, instead of believing in Christ, trust in themselves for salvation. 'Tis a common thing with men to take it upon themselves to purchase salvation for themselves, and so to do that great work that Christ came into the world to do. Are there none such here that trust in their own prayers, and their good conversations, and the pains they take in religion, and their reforming their lives,3 and denying themselves as they do, to recommend 'em to God, to make some atonement for their past sins, and to draw the heart of God to them?

Consider three.4 things:

1.5 You take upon you to do the work of the great savior of the world. How great a thing that is that you take upon you. You trust in your own doings to appease God for your sins, and to incline the heart of God to you. Though you are poor, worthless, vile, polluted worms of the dust, yet so arrogant are you that you take upon you

-- 335 --

that very work; that very work that the only begotten Son of God did when upon earth, and that he became man to capacitate himself for, and in order to which God spent four thousand years in all the great dispensations of his providence in the government of the world through all that time, aiming chiefly at this: to make way for Christ's coming to do this work.6 This is the work that you take upon yourself, and foolishly think yourself sufficient as if you were big enough for it,7 and as though your prayers and other performances were excellent enough for this purpose. Consider how vain is the thought you entertain of yourself. How must such arrogance appear in the sight of Christ, whom it cost so much to make a purchase of salvation, when it was not [to] be obtained even by him, though so great and glorious a person, at a cheaper rate than his wading through a sea of blood and passing through the midst of the furnace of God's wrath.8 And how vain must your arrogance appear in the sight of God when he sees you imagining yourself righteous9 enough, and your worthless, polluted performances excellent enough, for the accomplishing that work of his own Son, to prepare the way for which he was employed in ordering all the great affairs of the world for so many ages.

2.1 If there be ground for you to trust, as you [do], in your own righteousness, then all that Christ did to purchase salvation when on earth, and all that God did from the first fall of man to that time to prepare the way for it, is in vain. Your self-righteousness charges God with the greatest2 folly; as though he had done all things in vain, even so much in vain that he has done all this to bring about an accomplishment of that that you alone, a little worm with your poor polluted prayers, and the little pains you take in religion, mingled with all that hypocrisy and filthiness, was sufficient to accomplish for yourself without Christ's help. For if you can appease God's anger for your sins, [that] can or ought to be appeased, and you can commend yourself to God by these means, then you have no need of Christ, but he

-- 336 --

"is dead in vain," Galatians 2:21, "If righteousness come by the law, [then Christ is dead in vain]."

If you can do this by your prayers, Christ might have spared his pains; he might have spared his blood, he might have kept within the bosom of his Father without coming down into this evil world to be despised and reproached and persecuted to death. And God need not to have busied himself as he did for four thousand years together, causing so many changes in the state of the world all that while, in order to be bringing that about that you, as little as you are, can accomplish in3 a few days only, with the trouble of a few sighs, and groans, and prayers, and some other religious performances. Consider with yourself what greater folly could you have devised to have charged upon God than this, to do all those things before and after Christ came into the world so needlessly, when instead of all this he might only have called you forth and committed the business to you which you think you can do so easily.

Alas, how blind are natural men, how sottish are the thoughts they have of things, and especially how vain are the thoughts they have of themselves; how ignorant are they of themselves, how ignorant of their own littleness and pollution, how do they exalt themselves up to heaven, what great things do they assume to themselves.

34 You that trust in your own righteousness arrogate to yourself the honor of the greatest thing that ever God himself did, not only as if you were sufficient [to] do divine works, and to accomplish5 some of the great works of God, but such is your pride and vanity that you are not content without taking upon you to do the very greatest work that ever God himself wrought, even the Work of Redemption. You see by what has been said how God has subordinated all his other works to this work: how [his] works of providence are God's greatest, and how that all God's works of providence, from the beginning of the generations of men, were in order to this, to make way [for it].6

But this is what you take upon yourself. To take on yourself to work out redemption is a greater thing than if you took it upon you to create a world. Consider with yourself what a figure you, a poor

-- 337 --

worm, would make if you should seriously go about to create such a world as God did, and should swell in your own conceit7 of yourself, and deck yourself with majesty, and should pretend to speak the word of power and call an universe out of nothing, intending to go on in order and say, "Let there be light.… [Let there be a firmament.… Let the waters … be gathered together.]"8

But then consider that in attempting to work out redemption yourself, you attempt a greater thing than this, and are serious in it, and won't be beat off from it; but strive in it, and are full of the thought of yourself that you are sufficient for it, and always big with hopes of accomplishing of it. Yea, you take upon you [to] do the very greatest and most difficult part of this work, viz. to purchase redemption. Christ can accomplish other parts of this work without cost and without any trouble or difficulty, but this part cost him ‹his life›. But this is the part which self-righteous persons go about to accomplish for themselves. If all the angels in heaven had been sufficient for this work, would God have gone about to have done such things as he did in9 order to it before he sent his son into the world? And would he ever have sent his own Son, the creator and God of the angels, into the world to have done and suffered such things?

What self-righteous persons take to themselves is that same work that Christ was engaged in when he was in his agony and bloody sweat and when he died on the cross, which was the greatest thing that ever the eyes of angels beheld. This as great as it is they imagine that they can do; the same that Christ accomplished by it. Their self-righteousness does, in effect, charge Christ's offering up himself in these sufferings as the greatest instance of folly that ever men or angels saw, instead of being the most glorious display of divine wisdom and grace that ever was seen. Yea, self-righteousness makes all that Christ did through the whole course of his life, and all that he said and suffered for through that whole time, and his incarnation itself, and not only so, but all that God had been doing in the great dispensations of his providence from the beginning of the world to that time, as all nothing but a scene of the most wild,1 and extreme, and transcendent folly.

Is it any wonder then that a self-righteous spirit is so represented

-- 338 --

in Scripture, and spoken of as that which is most fatal to the souls of men. And is it any wonder that God is represented in Scripture as being so provoked with the Pharisees, and others that trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and were proud of their goodness, and thought that their own performances were a valuable price of God's favor and love. Let persons hence be warned against a self righteous spirit. You that are seeking your salvation and taking pains in religion, if there are any such here present, take heed to yourselves that you don't trust in what you do: That you don't harbor any such thoughts that God now seeing how you are reformed, how you take pains in religion, and how you are sometimes affected, will be pacified towards you with respect to your sins; And on the account of it will not be so angry for your former sins2 and that you shall gain on him by such things, and draw his heart to show you mercy. Or at least that God ought to accept of what you do, so as to be inclined by it in some measure to forgive you and have mercy on you. If you entertain this thought, that God is obliged to it and don't do justly if he refuse to regard your prayers and pains, and so quarrel with God and complain of it for not doing it, this shows what your opinion is of your own righteousness, viz. that 'tis a valuable price of salvation and ought to be accepted of God as such. Such complaining of God and quarreling with him for not taking more notice of your religion, plainly shows that [you] are guilty of all that arrogance that has been spoken of, thinking yourself sufficient to offer the price of your own salvation.

Thirdly.3 What has been said on this subject affords matter of reproof to those that carelessly neglect the salvation of Christ, such who live a senseless kind of life, neglecting4 their business of religion and their own precious souls for the present, not taking any course to get an interest in Christ, or what he has done and suffered, or any part in that glorious salvation he has purchased by that price; but rather have their minds taken up about the gains of the world or about the vanities and pleasures of youth. And make so light of what they hear from time to time of Christ's salvation that they for the present don't so much as seek after it. Let me here apply myself to you in some expostulatory interrogations.

-- 339 --

1.5 Shall so many prophets, and kings, and righteous [men] have their minds so much taken up with the prospect of the purchase of salvation being wrought out in ages long after their death, and will you so neglect it when actually accomplished? You have heard what great account the church of God in all ages made of the future redemption of Christ; how joyfully they expected it, how they spoke of it, how they studied and searched6 into these things, how they sung joyful songs about, and had their hearts greatly engaged about it and yet never expected to see it done, did not expect that it would be accomplished till many ages after their death, 1 Peter 1:10–12 ["Of which salvation the prophets have enquired and searched diligently, … what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, … the sufferings of Christ.… Which are now reported unto you"]. How much did Isaiah, and Daniel, and other prophets speak ‹concerning this redemption›. How was David's mind taken [up; he] declared all his salvation, 2 Samuel 23:5.7 How much did he employ his voice and harp,8 though they beheld it as yet accomplished, and it was to be so long a time. And before that, how did Abraham and other patriarchs rejoice; and even the saints before the flood, though so long future and so very faintly and obscurely revealed.

Now these things are declared to you as9 actually fulfilled. The church now has seen all accomplished, all those great things they so joyfully prophesied of, and you are abundantly shown how those things were accomplished, Matthew 13:17, "Verily I say unto you, many prophets.…"1 And yet when these things are thus abundantly set before you as already accomplished, how do you slight them, how light do you make of them, how little are they taken notice of by you, how unconcerned about them, following other things and not so much as feeling any interest in them. Indeed, your sin is extremely aggravated in the sight of God. God has put you under very great advantages for your eternal salvation, far greater than those saints of old enjoyed, under a more glorious dispensation, [with] a more clear revelation of Christ and his salvation.2

-- 340 --

2.3 Shall the angels be so engaged about this salvation of Christ ever since the fall of man, though they are not immediately concerned, and will you who need it and have it offered to you be so careless about it4 You have heard how the angels at first were subjected to Christ as mediator, and how they have all along been ministering spirits to him in this affair. They have in all the great dispensations you have heard of, from the beginning of the world, been active and as a flame of fire in this affair, being most diligently employed as ministering spirits to minister to Christ in this great affair of man's redemption. And when Christ came, how engaged were their minds. [They] came to Zacharias, and came to Mary, to Joseph.5 And how were their minds engaged in the time of the birth of Christ; whole multitude of heavenly hosts sang, and from time to time ministered to Christ when on earth: [at the] time of his temptation, [in his] agony, at his resurrection, [and at his] ascension. All things show that they were greatly engaged, and the Scripture informs us they pry into these things, 1 Peter 1:12, "Which things the angels [desire to look into]." And how are they represented in the Revelation6 as being employed in heaven in singing.7 Shall these take so much notice who don't need [it], have no immediate concern or interest in it, or offer of it; and shall you to whom it is offered—for [you] are in such extreme necessity—‹neglect and take no notice of it›?

3.8 Was it worth the while for Christ to labor so hard, and do and suffer so much, to procure this salvation; and is [it] not worth the while for you to be at some labor in seeking of it? Was it a thing of so great importance that salvation should be procured for sinners, as that it was worthy to lie with such weight on the mind of Christ as to induce him to ‹suffer even death itself›? Though he stood in need of nothing, though he was like to gain nothing of addition to his eternal happiness, get nothing by those that he saves, did not need 'em; was it of such importance that sinners should be saved that he might properly be induced to ‹submit to such humiliation and suffering›.

-- 341 --

And yet [is] it not worth the while for you9 who are one of those miserable sinners that need this salvation and must perish eternally without [it], to take earnest pains to obtain an interest in it after it is procured and all things are ready?

4.1 Shall the great God be so concerned about this salvation as so often to overturn the world to make way for it, and when all is done is it not worth your seeking after? How has the Lord of heaven and earth been, as it were, engaged about this affair; what great, what wonderful things has he done from one age to another, removing kings and setting up kings, raising up a great number of prophets, separating a distinct nation from the rest of the world, overturning one nation and kingdom and another, and often overturning the state of the world, and so continue bringing one change and revolution after another for forty centuries, or hundreds of years in succession, to make way? And when he has done all, and at the close of these ages, the great savior comes: and2 becoming incarnate, and passing through a long series of reproaches and suffering, and then suffering all the waves and billows of God's wrath for men's sin as they enveloped3 and passed over his soul; after all, is it not worthy of your taking so much notice of or being so much concerned about, though you are one of those persons that need this salvation; but that it should be thrown by and made nothing of in comparison of worldly gain, or gay clothing, or youthful diversions, and other such trifling things?

O that you that live negligent of this salvation would consider what you do; what you have had from this subject may show you what reason there is in that of the Apostle, Hebrews 2:3, "How shall we escape, if we neglect [so great salvation]." And in that Acts 13:41, "Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish." God looks on such as you as great enemies of the cross of Christ, and adversaries and despisers of all the glory of this great work. And if God4 has made such account of the glory of salvation as to destroy many nations, and so often to overturn all nations, to prepare the way for the glory to his Son in this affair, how little account will he make of the lives and souls of ten thousand such opposers and despisers as you, that continue impenitent

-- 342 --

in comparison of that glory. When he shall hereafter come and find that your welfare stands in the way of that glory, why surely you shall be dashed in pieces, as a potter's vessel, and trodden down as the mire of the streets.5 God may through wonderful patience bear with wicked, careless sinners for a while, but he will [not long] bear with such despisers of his dear Son and his great salvation, the glory of which he has had so much at heart, before he will utterly consume them without remedy or mercy.

6I will conclude with a second use of encouragement to burdened souls very briefly to put their trust in Christ for salvation. To all such as are not careless and negligent, but do make7 seeking an interest in Christ their main business, being sensible in some measure of their necessity of an interest, being afraid of the wrath to come; to such, what has been said on this subject holds forth great matter of encouragement to come and venture their souls in the Lord Jesus Christ. Here consider two things in particular.

1.8 The completeness of the purchase that has been made. As you have heard, this work of purchasing salvation was wholly finished during the time [of Christ's humiliation].9 So here is need of nothing more: the servants are now sent forth with the message which we have account of in Matthew 22:4 ["Behold, I have prepared my dinner: my oxen and my fatlings are killed, and all things are ready: come unto the marriage"]. Are your sins many and great, here is enough.1 There is no need of any righteousness of yours; come freely without money and without price; come naked; come as a poor condemned [sinner]; come cast yourself down at Jesus' feet, as one just condemned and most utterly helpless. Here is complete salvation.

2.2 For Christ to reject one that thus comes to him would be to frustrate all those great things that you have heard of, that God had wrought from the fall of man, all that Christ did and suffered: Christ's incarnation, all the great things done in preparation, for all was for that end, that those might be saved that come to Jesus. Therefore you may be sure Christ will not be backward; he don't desire to

-- 343 --

frustrate himself in his own work, it3 cost him too dear for that. God the Father won't refuse you, for he don't desire to frustrate himself in all that he did for so many hundreds and thousands of years. Come therefore, hearken to the sweet and earnest calls of Christ to your soul. Do as he invites, and as he commands you in Matthew 11:28–30, "Come unto me, all [ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest]. Take my yoke [upon you, and learn of me, … and ye shall find rest unto your souls]. For my yoke is easy, [and my burden is light]."4

-- 344 --

1No. 7: SERMON EIGHTEEN2
[For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation form generation to generation.] Isaiah 51:8
DOCTRINE
[The Work of Redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.]

3WE are come now to the third and last period of this whole space of time beginning with Christ's resurrection, and reaching to the end of the world, and would now show how the Work of Redemption was also carried on through this period from this proposition, that the space of time from the end of Christ's humiliation to the end of the world is all taken up in bringing about the great effect or success of Christ's purchase.

Not but that there were not great effects and glorious successes of Christ's purchase of redemption before, even from the beginning of the generations of men. But all that success of Christ's redemption that was before, was only preparatory and was by way of anticipation, as some few fruits are gathered before the harvest. There was no more success before Christ came than God saw needful to prepare the way for his coming.4 The proper time of the success or effect of Christ's purchase of redemption is after the purchase has been made; as the proper time for the world to enjoy the light of the sun is the day time after the sun is risen, though it may be that some small

-- 345 --

matter of it [is] reflected from the moon and planets before.5 And even the success of Christ's redemption while he himself was on earth was very small in comparison of what it was after the conclusion of the period of his humiliation. But Christ's having finished that greatest and most difficult of all works, the work of the purchase of redemption, now is come the time for obtaining the end of it and obtaining the glorious effect of it. This is the next work he goes about. Having gone through the whole course of his sufferings and humiliation, there is an end to all things of that nature; he is never to suffer6 any more, but now is the time for him to obtain the joy that was set before him.7 Having made his soul an offering for sin, now is the time for him to see his seed and to have a portion divided to him with the great and to divide the spoil with the strong.8

This is pointed out by the Scripture. One design of Christ in what he had done in his humiliation was to lay a foundation for the overthrow of Satan's kingdom; and now is come the time to effect it, as Christ a little before his crucifixion said, John 12:31, "Now is the judgment of this world: now shall the prince of this world be cast out."
